lead: Regular languages are closed under operations that build new languages from old ones. If L₁ and L₂ are regular, so are L₁ ∪ L₂, L₁L₂, L₁*, complement, intersection, difference and reversal. Closure matters because it lets you build complex patterns from simple automata and prove a language is regular without writing a fresh machine. Decision properties go further: algorithms answer emptiness, finiteness, membership and equivalence. These checks sit inside compilers, network filters and text search tools. A regular language is one accepted by a DFA or an NFA.
prereq: You need DFA and NFA from Unit 1 and Kleene's theorem from Chapter 2.5.

sections.h3: Closure means the result is still regular

blocks.text: Closure says an operation on regular languages produces another regular language. You prove closure by construction: give a machine for the result.

items: Union L₁ ∪ L₂: make an ε-NFA with a new start state and ε-edges to the start states of machines for L₁ and L₂. A string is accepted if either copy accepts.
Concatenation L₁L₂: add ε-edges from every final state of the L₁ machine to the start state of the L₂ machine. The old final states stop being final; the L₂ final states remain final.
Kleene star L₁*: add a new start state that is also final, an ε-edge to the old start, and ε-edges from old final states back to the old start. This allows zero or more copies.

Complement: take a DFA for L, add one nonfinal dead state for the missing transitions (with self-loops on every symbol) so the machine becomes complete, then swap final and nonfinal states. The dead state becomes final, which is correct because every string that falls off the original machine is in the complement.
Intersection and difference: build the product DFA. For L₁ ∩ L₂, accept pairs final in both. For L₁ − L₂, accept pairs final in L₁ and nonfinal in L₂. Difference is L₁ ∩ complement(L₂).
Reversal Lᴿ: reverse every transition, make the old start state final, add a new start state with ε-edges to every old final state. The result is an ε-NFA, so Lᴿ is regular.

blocks.text: These constructions are enough; no counting argument is needed.
For DFAs A = (Q_A, Σ, δ_A, q_A, F_A) and B = (Q_B, Σ, δ_B, q_B, F_B), the product DFA P has states Q_A × Q_B. The start state is (q_A, q_B). On symbol a, δ_P((p, q), a) = (δ_A(p, a), δ_B(q, a)).

blocks.where: |Q_P| is the number of product states; |Q_A| and |Q_B| are the numbers of states in the two input DFAs.

blocks.text: Complete both A and B with nonfinal dead states before building the product, for every operation (union, intersection, difference). Then δ_P is total and the final-state rule for the chosen operation is sound. Choose final states: intersection final if both; union if either; difference if first final and second not.
Emptiness: L(P) = ∅ iff no final state is reachable from the start state. Run BFS or DFS on the product graph. A final state that exists but cannot be reached does not make the language nonempty.

Finiteness: L(P) is finite iff no cycle lies on a path from the start state to a final state. Mark useful states: reachable from start and able to reach a final state. If any useful state has a cycle through useful states, the language is infinite; if the useful part is acyclic, it is finite.

Membership asks whether a given string w is in L. For a DFA, start at q₀ and read symbols left to right. After |w| steps, accept iff the final state is in F. Time is O(|w|). For an NFA, simulate by carrying the set of possible states: O(|w| × |Q| × |Σ|), where |Q| is the number of NFA states and |Σ| is the alphabet size. Converting to a DFA first is also correct but can cost up to 2<sup>|Q|</sup> states, so simulate unless you need the DFA anyway.

Equivalence asks whether L(A) = L(B). Complete both DFAs, then build the product. A pair (p, q) is a mismatch if exactly one of p, q is final. Run BFS from (q_A, q_B). If a mismatch is reachable, the languages differ; that reachable string is a witness. If no mismatch is reachable, the languages are equal. The same search decides inclusion by looking for a reachable pair with p final and q nonfinal.
The symmetric-difference view is L(A) Δ L(B) = (L(A) ∩ complement L(B)) ∪ (complement L(A) ∩ L(B)). The languages are equal exactly when this union is empty.

Complete DFA is the repeated requirement. A missing transition kills the run: the string is rejected. If you swap final and nonfinal states without adding the dead state, those runs still die after swapping, so strings that belong to the complement are wrongly rejected. Add one nonfinal dead state for all missing transitions, make it loop on every symbol, then swap. Swapping finals of an NFA is the case that wrongly accepts strings, because different runs of the same string end in different states. Convert NFA to DFA first using subset construction, and keep the dead state.

examples.question: Let L₁ = {w ∈ {0,1}* : w has an even number of 0s} and L₂ = {w ∈ {0,1}* : w ends in 1}. Build the product DFA for L₁ ∩ L₂ and decide whether L₁ ∩ L₂ is empty. If it is not empty, give one string in it.
steps: DFA A for L₁ has states E (even 0s, start and final) and O (odd 0s, nonfinal). Transitions: E--0→O, E--1→E, O--0→E, O--1→O.
DFA B for L₂ has states N (last symbol not 1, start and nonfinal) and F (last symbol 1, final). Transitions: N--0→N, N--1→F, F--0→N, F--1→F.
Start state is (E,N). A final state for intersection needs both parts final: A final is E, B final is F, so only (E,F) is final.
Transitions: (E,N) on 0 → (O,N), on 1 → (E,F). (E,F) on 0 → (O,N), on 1 → (E,F). (O,N) on 0 → (E,N), on 1 → (O,F). (O,F) on 0 → (E,N), on 1 → (O,F).

(E,F) is reachable: (E,N) --0→ (O,N) --0→ (E,N) --1→ (E,F). So L₁ ∩ L₂ is not empty. The shortest witness is 1, because step 5 shows (E,N) --1→ (E,F) directly. The longer path 001 also works; this longer path is only to show reachability.
The path spells 001. It has two 0s and ends in 1, so 001 ∈ L₁ ∩ L₂. The shortest witness is 1.
examples.answer: The product has 4 states; L₁ ∩ L₂ is not empty; the shortest witness is 1; 001 (length 3) also works.

traps: Complementing an NFA by swapping final and nonfinal states is wrong. Convert to a DFA and complete it with a dead state first.
Product final states differ by operation: both final for intersection, either final for union, first final and second nonfinal for difference.
Emptiness depends on reachable final states. A final state that exists but cannot be reached from the start does not make the language nonempty.
Finiteness checks cycles on useful states that are reachable from start and can reach a final state. A cycle in an unreachable part of the DFA does not matter.
Equivalence needs a reachable-pair check. Comparing only the start states or only the final-state counts can miss a difference.

quiz.q: List four operations under which regular languages are closed.
quiz.a: Any four of union, concatenation, Kleene star, complement, intersection, difference, reversal.

quiz.q: Why is a complete DFA needed before complementing a regular language?
quiz.a: A missing transition means the DFA has no defined state for that input. Completing it adds a dead state. Swapping final and nonfinal then correctly rejects every string that enters the dead state.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the product starts at (E,N). What product state is reached after reading 001, and is it final?
quiz.a: Start (E,N); 0 gives (O,N); 0 gives (E,N); 1 gives (E,F). (E,F) is final for the intersection, so 001 is accepted.

quiz.q: A DFA has a final state q_f that is not reachable from the start state. Is its language empty? Explain.
quiz.a: Not necessarily. Emptiness requires that no final state is reachable. The unreachable q_f does not matter; check reachable final states only. If some other final state is reachable, the language is nonempty.

quiz.q: A reachable state q₁ has a cycle q₁ --a→ q₁, and q₁ can reach a final state. Is the language necessarily infinite?
quiz.a: Yes. Repeat the cycle a any number of times, then follow the path to the final state. This gives infinitely many accepted strings.

quiz.q: How does the symmetric-difference test decide whether L(A) = L(B)?
quiz.a: Form L(A) Δ L(B). The languages are equal exactly when this symmetric difference is empty. Emptiness is decided by checking whether any final state is reachable in the product construction for the symmetric difference.

quiz.q: A student checks two DFAs for equivalence by comparing only their start states and final-state sets. Give a counterexample idea.
quiz.a: Both DFAs can have the same start-state final status but differ after one symbol. For example, one accepts only strings ending in 1 and the other accepts only strings ending in 0, with both start states nonfinal. The product search finds a reachable mismatch; start-state comparison does not.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, closure and decision procedures appear in regular-expression engines, network intrusion filters and hardware verification. Tools simplify automata and check equivalence before chip fabrication. Search terms: automata library, DFA minimization, regular language inclusion, model checking finite-state systems.
